n: This topic is an introduction to forensic thanatology. Thanatology, from the Greek thanatos, death, is the branch of pathology that studies death and the processes associated with it. Forensic medicine mainly studies violent death, so the questions of thanatology occupy a central place in it. This knowledge is compulsory for every physician who may be drawn into the actions of a forensic medical expert or into a forensic examination.

First, the definitions of death. Death is the process of irreversible loss by the cerebral cortex of the ability to carry out higher nervous activity. This is the concept of brain death. The traditional definition is different: a persistent, irreversible cessation of the basic functions of the organism and of the indices of homeostasis. This is vegetative death. Partial death, that is, necrosis, is the irreversible disorganisation of a part of a living organism. Thus the concept of death is used in several senses.

Categories and kinds of death. By socio-legal criterion, death is non-violent, that is, from disease, or violent, that is, from external action. The kinds of violent death are homicide, suicide and accident. Remember: determining the category and kind lies within the competence not of the expert but of the investigating officers.

The cause of death is divided into three levels. The cause of death is an injury or disease that, by itself or through its complications, led to death. Establishing the cause is the main task of the forensic medical expert. First the immediate cause is determined, for example cerebral or pulmonary oedema, or shock. Then the intermediate cause is established, for example peritonitis or suppuration of a wound. Finally comes the underlying cause, that is, the underlying disease or injury, for example a skull fracture or an acute ulcer.

t: Case analysis: the chain of causes
n: Case analysis: the chain of causes. Example: in a perforated gastric ulcer, peritonitis develops; peritonitis here is the intermediate cause. The ulcer disease is the underlying cause, while the immediate cause is the morphological equivalent of the terminal disturbance, for example shock. Ask yourself: by what term would you name each link of this chain?

t: Structure of the forensic medical diagnosis
n: The structure of the forensic medical diagnosis. The forensic medical diagnosis is a set of judgements about injuries and diseases, written in pathogenetic sequence. It consists of three parts. The first is the underlying disease or injury. The second is its complications. The third is concomitant diseases. The diagnosis takes into account not only the cause but also the mechanism of death.

The mechanism of death is called thanatogenesis. Thanatogenesis is the sequence of structural and functional disturbances, caused by disease or injury, that leads to death. According to thanatogenesis, death is divided into kinds such as death from brain, lung, heart, kidney, liver and adrenal gland failure. By frequency, the cardiovascular variant of thanatogenesis stands first.

Cardiovascular thanatogenesis. If the heart or vessels cannot ensure haemodynamics, circulation stops, and general hypoxia and irreversible changes are observed. Many morphological changes in this area existed during life and may not be directly related to death. In forensic medicine acute, and less often subacute, heart failure is frequently encountered.

t: Death from lung, brain and kidney failure
n: Death from lung, brain and kidney failure. In pulmonary death, obstacles to gas exchange are observed: pneumosclerosis, bronchospasm, exudate inside the alveoli, and there may also be cor pulmonale. Cerebral death is characterised by processes in the CNS or the meninges: tumour, encephalitis, brain contusion, haematomas. In renal death, widespread kidney damage is found: nephrosclerosis, pyelonephritis, glomerulonephritis, amyloidosis.

By speed, the process of dying most often consists of 5 stages. The first stage is the preagonal, the initial stage. The second is the terminal pause, when breathing stops. The third is agony, the last attempt. The fourth is clinical death: consciousness, breathing and cardiac activity are absent, but resuscitation is still possible. The fifth is biological death, an irreversible disturbance of the structure and function of the brain.

Agony is the set of pathophysiological processes reflecting a disturbance in the coordination of the homeostatic systems of the organism. Injuries received during the period of agony are called agonal; the reaction to them is weaker than to injuries received in other periods of life. Death occurring without agony, or with very brief agony, in apparent good health, is called sudden death, that is, skoropostizhnaya.

Quick questions on cause and mechanism. First question: in what order are the immediate, intermediate and underlying causes determined? Answer: first the immediate, then the intermediate and the underlying. Second question: which variant of thanatogenesis is encountered most often? Answer: the cardiovascular.

Signs of rapidly occurring death. In rapid death the blood in the heart and vessels is fluid, there is venous congestion in the internal organs, and the cadaveric lividity is diffuse. Pinpoint haemorrhages are seen on the serous and mucous membranes, and autolysis in the pancreas. In slow death, by contrast, if the agony was prolonged, postmortem blood clots are numerous and rich in fibrin, and dystrophy is also found.

The main sign of death is an irreversible change in the structure and function of the brain. This includes the absence of electrical activity on the EEG and damage to neurons. In severe cerebral oedema or perifocal oedematous haemorrhages in vital structures, death can be confirmed morphologically. All the other signs are a consequence of irreversible damage to the homeostatic systems.

t: Signs for establishing the fact of death
n: Signs for establishing the fact of death. There is no consciousness or reflexes, that is, the corneal and pupillary reflexes. There is no electrical activity on the EEG and ECG. There is no pulse, heartbeat or breathing. Beloglazov's sign: when the eyeball is pressed, the pupil takes an oval shape; this is a reliable criterion of death and appears in 10–15 minutes. However, only cadaveric changes are considered indubitable signs.

Sarkisov's law: when a biological system is disrupted, the higher levels are lost first, then the lower ones in succession. Consequently, the homeostatic coordination of organ functions is disturbed first, then that of individual organs and tissues. For this reason the temporary survival of tissues is the cause of the existence of supravital reactions. The sequence: higher level, lower level, homeostasis, tissue and the supravital state.

Supravital reactions. The electromechanical reactions of muscles disappear within 8–12 hours. Under the action of electric current, the whole face contracts at 2–3 hours, and only the orbicularis oris muscle at 3–5 hours. The pupillary reaction to drugs persists for up to 1.5 days, and the reaction of the sweat glands for 20 hours.

The first of the early cadaveric changes is cooling. Cooling of the body is due to heat loss continuing while the production of endogenous heat has stopped; the temperature falls on average by 1 °C per hour. Exposed parts of the body cool faster. Temperature is measured in the axilla, the rectum and the liver tissue. The result of thermometry is usually assessed together with other findings; corrections for clothing and weight are taken into account.

Cadaveric desiccation is the result of continuing evaporation of water from the skin and mucous membranes and the cessation of glandular secretion. Areas without a stratum corneum dry fastest: the sclera, the red border of the lips and the surface of abrasions. In open eyes, after 4–5 hours the cornea becomes cloudy, and Larcher spots appear on the sclera.

Rigor mortis is associated with the redistribution of calcium and the polymerisation of actomyosin; it begins in 2–6 hours. In the classical view, descending from the masticatory muscles downward, it reaches its maximum in 12–24 hours. From the middle of the second day it begins to disappear, and on days 3–7 it disappears completely. Remember the dynamics in this order: onset, maximum, beginning of disappearance and complete disappearance.

Factors affecting rigor. Rigor is pronounced in those who did physical work, in large blood loss, and in those who died in a convulsive period. In children, the elderly and in some poisonings, for example by the death cap mushroom, it is weak. Rigor of the heart begins in 2–3 hours and persists for 1.5–2 days; if the heart has not gone into rigor, cardiac thanatogenesis is assumed.

t: Rigor and the position of the body
n: Rigor and the position of the body. If rigor is artificially broken in the first hours, it is restored, but more weakly. If the degree of rigor does not correspond to the time determined by other signs, this is significant. If there is no rigor in the upper limbs but there is in the lower ones, the position of the body has been changed.

Cadaveric lividity passes through three stages. Hypostasis appears at 2–4 hours: on pressure it disappears, and if the body is turned it shifts. Stasis at 12–24 hours: on pressure it blanches; if the body is turned over, two groups of patches appear. Imbibition at about the second day: on pressure the colour does not change, and the location does not change either.

t: Colour of cadaveric lividity and hypostasis
n: The colour of cadaveric lividity depends on the cause. In smoke gas poisoning it is bright red, in cyanides cherry-red, and with methaemoglobin-forming agents grey-brown. In those who died from cold and in bodies in water, a pinkish-red colour is observed. Cadaveric hypostasis, in turn, is postmortem blood filling of the lower parts of the internal organs.

t: Case analysis: lividity divided into two groups
n: Case analysis: lividity divided into two groups. A body was found; there is cadaveric lividity on its back and also on its sides. At the stage of stasis, that is, 12–24 hours, if the position is changed, part of the blood shifts and the old patches remain. Question: what does this situation show, and what can be said about the time of death?

Blood clotting and autolysis. After death the blood is fluid; in prolonged agony it may clot after 2 hours, whereas in rapid death it remains fluid owing to fibrinolysis. Autolysis is the breakdown of tissues by their own proteolytic enzymes; first the mucosa of the gastrointestinal tract and the pancreas are affected. Histological assessment of autolysis is used to determine the age of death; after 6 hours a disturbance of blood distribution appears.

t: Simpson: rigor and time of death
n: According to Simpson, on rigor and time of death. Rigor is a temperature-dependent change occurring in muscle cells because of lack of oxygen. In moderate conditions it is detected in the face at 1–4 and in the limbs at 3–6 hours; the maximum is at about 18 hours. Rigor does not give an exact time of death; tables should be treated with caution.

t: Simpson: temperature and the Henssge nomogram
n: According to Simpson, on temperature and the Henssge nomogram. For temperature, 3 assumptions are made: 37 °C at the moment of death, extrapolation is possible, and the ambient temperature is constant. In the Henssge nomogram the limit of 95% accuracy is at most 2.8 hours on either side of the most probable time. The nomogram takes into account body temperature, ambient temperature, body weight and corrections. A change in ambient temperature of 5 °C can change the time of death by at least 1 hour.

The first of the late changes is putrefaction. Putrefaction is the breakdown of organic substances, especially proteins, under the action of bacteria. An odour is noticeable as early as the first day; green discolouration begins from the iliac region: in summer at the end of the first day, in winter on days 2–3. Then the putrefactive venous network and emphysema appear, and the body swells with gas.

The body and insects. Flies lay eggs; in 1–2 days larvae emerge and eat the tissues. In about a week the larvae pupate; in 7–10 days the adult fly emerges. The length of the larva is measured, which is larvometry; it corresponds to age. Then beetles come.

Preservative processes. Adipocere forms in an environment with little oxygen and high moisture; it is fully formed in about 1 year. Mummification occurs in a dry, ventilated place; in an adult it does not occur earlier than 2–3 months. In a peat bog, humic acids soften the bone, and the microstructure is preserved for a long time.

t: Other methods of determining time of death
n: There are other methods of determining the time of death as well. If a more precise time is required, indices such as the pH of blood and vitreous humour and the concentrations of potassium and calcium ions are studied. In addition, hypoxanthine, creatinine, DNA degradation and enzyme activity in the vitreous humour are measured. The most accurate result is given by applying a complex of different methods.

t: The concept of the scene of an incident
n: The concept of the scene of an incident. The scene of an incident is the place or room where an event requiring legal assessment took place and which is subjected to an investigative examination. The discovery of a body is itself an incident, so the place where a body is found is always a scene of an incident. Examining the body at the scene is part of the examination of the scene; participants are the investigator and two witnesses.

Duties of the specialist physician. The specialist is a forensic medical expert or a physician with special knowledge; he must have no interest in the outcome of the case. His duties: to record death or provide first aid; to describe the position of the body, clothing and appearance. Also to describe the cadaveric phenomena and injuries, to assist in collecting biological evidence, and to give oral answers.

t: Static and dynamic stages of the examination
n: The static and dynamic stages of the examination. In the static stage the scene is studied without disturbing it, described without touching objects and photographed. The body remains in place; its location and the arrangement of the body parts, that is, the posture, are recorded. In the dynamic stage the objects are picked up and carefully studied in rubber gloves, and the examination of the body is carried out.

t: Order of examining the body in the dynamic stage
n: The order of examining the body in the dynamic stage. First, it begins with the clothing; clothing is not removed on the spot, except when taken as evidence. Second, the general description: sex, age, build, height. Third, the cadaveric phenomena are examined by the standard. Fourth, the record: cooling, Larcher spots, cadaveric lividity, rigor, muscle reactions and rectal temperature are written down.

Describing injuries. Natural orifices, foreign bodies, the external genitalia and the bones are examined without rough movements. The site of the injury is indicated precisely; the kind, that is, abrasion, bruise or wound, the shape, colour and size are described. A wound is described by the clock face. Remember: a wound must not be probed, because a false track is created.

t: What cannot be decided at the scene
n: What can and cannot be decided at the scene. At the scene the exact time of death cannot be stated, but an opinion can be given as to whether the time indicated by a witness is possible. The cause of death is decided only after a full forensic medical examination of the body. The group characteristics of a weapon are determined in the mortuary; at the scene, however, certain weapons can be excluded.

t: Place where a newborn is found
n: The place where a newborn is found. The bodies of foetuses or newborns are found in different places; often they are wrapped in a newspaper, a sheet or clothing. Objects found with the body are described in detail; inscriptions, stamps and marks are sought and it is established to whom they belong. The objects are preserved and handed over to the investigating authorities.
